basic_information.name: Chroma
basic_information.creator: Chroma Inc. (San Francisco, CA), co-founded by Jeff Huber and Anton Troynikov
basic_information.description: Chroma is an open-source, AI-native embedding database designed for developer simplicity and rapid prototyping of LLM-powered applications. Python-native with a focus on ergonomic APIs, Chroma provides vector search (HNSW), full-text search (BM25/SPLADE), and metadata filtering in a lightweight package. Its core has been rewritten in Rust for performance (4x faster writes/queries), and it supports multimodal embeddings via OpenCLIP. Chroma is the most popular open-source vector database by PyPI downloads (8M+/month) and is deeply integrated into the LangChain and LlamaIndex ecosystems, making it the default choice for AI developers building their first RAG system.
basic_information.release_date: Company founded April 2022; public launch February 2023; latest version v1.4.1 released January 14, 2026
basic_information.github_stars: ~16,000-25,000 stars on GitHub (as of February 2026; sources vary, likely ~16k-17k core repo with broader ecosystem citations higher)

technical_architecture.architecture_type: Hybrid in-memory and disk-based architecture. Supports ephemeral (in-memory), persistent (disk-backed), client/server (HTTP), and cloud (serverless) modes. Originally Python-native with SQLite for metadata/documents and HNSW for vector indexing. Major Rust-core rewrite in 2025 delivers 4x faster writes/queries with multithreading (eliminates Python GIL bottleneck). Serverless cloud architecture backed by object storage for terabyte-scale data.
technical_architecture.language: Rust (core engine, post-2025 rewrite), Python (primary SDK and original implementation); client SDKs in Python, TypeScript/JavaScript, Go, Ruby, Java, Elixir, Dart, PHP, Rust (community clients)
technical_architecture.embedding_dimensions: Supports arbitrary embedding dimensions. Works with all major embedding model outputs (384, 768, 1024, 1536, 3072+). No hard upper limit documented; dimension set at collection creation.
technical_architecture.indexing_algorithm: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) as primary vector index with configurable parameters (ef_construction, ef_search, M). SQLite FTS5 for full-text/lexical search. Supports BM25 and SPLADE for sparse vector search. No native product quantization or binary quantization support (unlike Qdrant/Milvus).
technical_architecture.scalability: Comfortable handling tens of millions of embeddings with flat query latency (~3ms regardless of dataset size from 500 to 10K+ documents). Tested stable up to ~7M embeddings in benchmarks. Rust rewrite enables billion-scale embeddings in principle. Cloud version supports terabyte-scale with object-storage-backed serverless architecture. Single-node architecture for self-hosted; distributed only via Chroma Cloud. No native sharding or horizontal scaling for self-hosted deployments.
technical_architecture.deployment_options: Local in-process (ephemeral or persistent), Docker container, Chroma Cloud (fully managed serverless), BYOC (Bring Your Own Cloud in customer VPC), Railway/Render/Fly.io one-click deploys. Kubernetes deployment possible but not officially supported with Helm charts. Available on Docker Hub (mcp/chroma image).

rag_specific_capabilities.retrieval_method: Dense vector search (cosine similarity, L2, inner product via HNSW), sparse vector search (BM25, SPLADE), full-text search (SQLite FTS5), regex search, metadata filtering with $and/$or operators, and hybrid queries combining vector + full-text + metadata. Supports where and where_document filtering clauses.
rag_specific_capabilities.chunking_strategy_support: Chroma is a storage/retrieval layer and is agnostic to chunking strategy. Integrates with LangChain (RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter, SemanticChunker), LlamaIndex (SentenceSplitter, SemanticSplittingNodeParser), and Unstructured for fixed-size, semantic, recursive, and document-structure-aware chunking. Users implement chunking via orchestration frameworks before inserting into Chroma.
rag_specific_capabilities.reranking_support: No built-in reranking engine. Relies on orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex) for cross-encoder reranking or score fusion. Can combine dense and sparse search results manually. No native ColBERT late-interaction support.
rag_specific_capabilities.multimodal_support: Built-in OpenCLIP embedding function for unified text and image embeddings in a single collection. Supports multimodal collections that can store and be queried by multiple modalities. Additional embedding functions for Cohere, OpenAI, Jina, VoyageAI, and Roboflow. Users can bring custom multimodal embedding functions.
rag_specific_capabilities.graph_rag_support: No native knowledge graph or GraphRAG support. Chroma is a pure vector/document store. GraphRAG implementations require pairing Chroma with a graph database (e.g., Neo4j). Community examples exist but no official integration.
rag_specific_capabilities.citation_grounding: No built-in citation generation or grounding verification. Documents and metadata are stored alongside embeddings, allowing downstream citation via the orchestration layer. Source attribution must be implemented by the application using Chroma's metadata return capabilities.
rag_specific_capabilities.context_window_optimization: No built-in context window management. Relies on orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex) for context selection, compression, and summarization. Chroma's efficient top-k retrieval and metadata filtering help select the most relevant chunks to fit within LLM context windows.

performance_and_benchmarks.latency: ~3ms query latency regardless of dataset size (500 to 10,000+ documents). Flat latency profile is a key strength. Post-Rust-rewrite: 4x faster writes and queries compared to Python implementation. Suitable for real-time applications with human users.
performance_and_benchmarks.throughput: Specific QPS benchmarks not widely published by Chroma. The Rust rewrite with multithreading eliminates GIL bottleneck, enabling parallel query processing. Supports Apache Arrow data format and base64 vector encoding for optimized data transmission. [uncertain]
performance_and_benchmarks.accuracy_metrics: HNSW is an approximate nearest neighbor algorithm; recall is configurable via ef_search parameter. Higher ef_search = higher recall but slower queries. No published MTEB or BEIR scores (Chroma is a database, not an embedding model). Accuracy depends on the embedding model used, not Chroma itself.
performance_and_benchmarks.benchmark_results: In VectorDBBench (Zilliz), Chroma performed well up to ~7M embeddings. Query latency remains flat at ~3ms. Compared to competitors: generally slower than Qdrant and Milvus at large scale (>1M vectors) due to single-node architecture. Competitive for small-to-medium workloads. No native quantization means higher memory usage per vector than Qdrant (binary quantization) or Milvus (PQ). [uncertain]

integration_and_ecosystem.framework_compatibility: LangChain (langchain-chroma v1.1.0+ package, first-class integration), LlamaIndex (llama-index-vector-stores-chroma v0.5.5+), Haystack (ChromaDocumentStore), DSPy (via dspy-ai[chromadb] extra), Microsoft Semantic Kernel (official Chroma connector), CrewAI, AutoGen, AnythingLLM, and Spring AI. One of the most widely integrated vector databases across AI frameworks.
integration_and_ecosystem.model_compatibility: Model-agnostic — works with any embedding model. Built-in embedding functions for: OpenAI (text-embedding-ada-002, text-embedding-3-small/large), Cohere (embed-english-v3.0), Jina AI, VoyageAI, Roboflow, and OpenCLIP (multimodal). Default embedding function uses sentence-transformers (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). Compatible with Anthropic, Google, Mistral, and all Hugging Face models via custom embedding functions.
integration_and_ecosystem.mcp_integration_status: Official MCP server available (chroma-core/chroma-mcp on GitHub). Supports ephemeral, persistent, HTTP, and cloud client types. Provides collection management, document operations, semantic search, full-text search, and metadata filtering tools. Compatible with Claude, Cursor, and other MCP-compatible AI agents. Available on PyPI as chroma-mcp-server and Docker Hub as mcp/chroma.
integration_and_ecosystem.data_source_connectors: No built-in data source connectors. Chroma focuses on the storage/retrieval layer. Data ingestion is handled by orchestration frameworks: LangChain document loaders (S3, GCS, Confluence, Notion, Slack, web crawl, PDF, etc.), LlamaIndex readers (100+ data sources via LlamaHub), Unstructured (document processing), and Airbyte (300+ source connectors). Users build ingestion pipelines externally.
integration_and_ecosystem.observability_integration: No built-in observability or tracing. Chroma Cloud provides a web dashboard for collection management and usage monitoring. For tracing, relies on orchestration-layer integrations: LangSmith, Langfuse, and Arize Phoenix via LangChain/LlamaIndex OpenTelemetry instrumentation. No native Prometheus metrics or Grafana dashboard support for self-hosted deployments.

pricing_and_cost.pricing_model: Open-core model: open-source database (Apache 2.0) is completely free. Chroma Cloud uses serverless, usage-based pricing that scales linearly from $0. Enterprise tier (BYOC) with custom SLAs available.
pricing_and_cost.free_tier: $5 in free credits on Chroma Cloud (setup in under 30 seconds). Self-hosted is completely free with no limits. Open-source version has no restrictions on vectors, collections, or queries.
pricing_and_cost.cost_at_scale: Chroma Cloud: usage-based pricing starting at $0, scaling linearly. Enterprise tier offers $100 in credits then usage-based pricing. Specific per-vector or per-GB pricing not publicly detailed as of February 2026. Self-hosted: infrastructure costs only (a small VM at ~$20-50/month can handle millions of vectors). Significantly cheaper than Pinecone at equivalent scale. [uncertain]
pricing_and_cost.total_cost_of_ownership: Self-hosted: free software + infrastructure (e.g., $20-100/month for a VM handling 1-10M vectors). No embedding generation costs if using default sentence-transformers model (runs on CPU). With OpenAI embeddings: add ~$0.02-0.13 per 1M tokens. Chroma's lightweight architecture means lower compute requirements than Milvus or Weaviate. Main TCO advantage: zero licensing cost, simple single-node deployment reduces ops overhead. Main TCO risk: no horizontal scaling for self-hosted means potential re-architecture at large scale. [uncertain]

adoption_and_market.market_position: Most popular open-source vector database by developer adoption (8M+ PyPI downloads/month). Market leader for prototyping and small-to-medium RAG applications. Strong challenger positioning but not yet an enterprise-grade competitor to Pinecone, Qdrant, or Milvus for billion-scale production workloads. Positioned as the 'SQLite of vector databases' — lightweight, embedded, developer-first.
adoption_and_market.notable_customers: Used extensively in the AI developer community and startup ecosystem. Featured in OpenAI Cookbook tutorials. Widely adopted by LangChain and LlamaIndex users as default vector store. Specific enterprise customer names not prominently publicized. Primary adoption is among individual developers, startups, and research teams rather than large enterprises. [uncertain]
adoption_and_market.community_size: ~16,000-25,000 GitHub stars, 10,000+ Discord members, ~1.7-1.9M monthly PyPI downloads, ~212K monthly npm downloads, 3,837+ commits, used in 90K+ open-source repositories on GitHub. Active cookbook and documentation ecosystem.
adoption_and_market.funding_and_valuation: Total funding: ~$20.3M over 2 rounds. Pre-seed: ~$2.3M (May 2022, led by Anthony Goldbloom/AIX Ventures, James Cham/Bloomberg Beta, Nat Friedman & Daniel Gross/AI Grant). Seed: $18M (April 2023, led by Quiet Capital). Additional unattributed VC round in February 2024. Valuation: ~$75M (as of seed round). No Series A announced as of February 2026.
adoption_and_market.competitive_landscape: Direct competitors: Pinecone (fully managed, proprietary, zero-ops but higher cost), Qdrant (Rust-based, advanced filtering, better at scale), Milvus/Zilliz (C++, highest throughput at billion-scale), Weaviate (Go-based, strong hybrid search, modular). Indirect competitors: pgvector (PostgreSQL extension, familiar to backend devs), Redis Vector Search, Elasticsearch vector search. Chroma differentiates via: simplest developer experience, Python-native API, fastest time-to-first-query, best framework integration coverage, and lowest barrier to entry.

entrepreneurial_relevance.startup_applicability: Best for: solo developers, hackathon projects, early-stage startups (pre-seed to seed), and teams of 1-10 building their first AI/RAG product. Ideal when time-to-market matters more than scale. Perfect for MVPs and POCs where you need semantic search working in minutes, not days. Budget: $0 for self-hosted (just infrastructure), $5 free credits on Cloud. Use case fit: conversational AI memory, semantic document search, Q&A chatbots, recommendation systems, RAG-powered knowledge bases. Not recommended for: billion-vector workloads, multi-tenant SaaS at scale, or workloads requiring advanced filtering and quantization from day one.
entrepreneurial_relevance.build_vs_buy_guidance: Self-host (free) when: team is Python-proficient, dataset < 10M vectors, single-tenant application, cost sensitivity is high. Use Chroma Cloud when: want zero infrastructure management, need collaboration features (dashboard, API keys), scaling beyond single-node limits. Consider migrating to Qdrant/Pinecone/Milvus when: dataset exceeds 10M vectors, need horizontal scaling, require advanced quantization, or multi-tenant architecture is critical. The migration cost from Chroma is relatively low since all major frameworks abstract the vector store layer.
entrepreneurial_relevance.time_to_production: POC: 30 minutes to 1 day (pip install chromadb + 10 lines of Python). MVP with RAG pipeline: 2-5 days using LangChain or LlamaIndex. Production deployment on Chroma Cloud: 1-2 weeks including testing. Self-hosted production: 2-4 weeks including Docker deployment, monitoring setup, and performance tuning. Fastest time-to-first-query of any vector database.
key_lessons: 1. Start with Chroma for speed, plan migration path for scale — Chroma gets you to a working RAG demo faster than any alternative (30 minutes), but architect your code with framework abstractions (LangChain/LlamaIndex) so you can swap to Qdrant or Pinecone when you outgrow single-node limits.

2. The embedding model matters more than the vector database — at prototype scale, the quality of your embeddings (OpenAI vs. sentence-transformers vs. Cohere) has far more impact on RAG quality than database choice. Invest time in embedding selection and chunking strategy before optimizing the database.

3. Use Chroma's multimodal support to differentiate — built-in OpenCLIP support for text + image embeddings in a single collection enables multimodal RAG prototypes that competitors require more setup to achieve.

4. Beware the scaling cliff — Chroma works beautifully for < 1M vectors on a single node, but has no native horizontal scaling for self-hosted deployments. Plan your migration trigger (dataset size, QPS requirements, multi-tenancy needs) before you hit the cliff.

5. Leverage the ecosystem, not just the database — Chroma's real moat is its integration depth with LangChain, LlamaIndex, OpenAI Cookbook, and every AI tutorial on the internet. This means more community examples, faster debugging, and easier hiring of developers who already know the stack.
entrepreneurial_relevance.no_code_interface: Chroma Cloud provides a web dashboard for collection management, API key generation, and usage monitoring. No built-in no-code RAG pipeline builder. Third-party GUI tools available: VectorAdmin (universal vector DB GUI), Chroma Flow Studio (Python GUI), Chroma Explorer (macOS desktop app), ChromaDB Admin UI (Next.js web UI), and Chromagraphic. AnythingLLM provides a no-code interface with Chroma as a backend vector store option.
entrepreneurial_relevance.session_mapping: Session 2 (Prompt engineering & no-code tools — hands-on RAG demo with Chroma) and Session 3 (Framing & managing AI projects — Build vs Buy database decisions, scaling considerations)

confidence.data_quality: High — information sourced from official Chroma documentation (docs.trychroma.com), GitHub repository, Crunchbase/Tracxn funding data, PyPI download statistics, and independent comparison articles from Airbyte, Firecrawl, and AIMultiple.
confidence.cross_reference: Funding confirmed by Crunchbase, Tracxn, SiliconANGLE, and Clay. GitHub stars and release versions verified via GitHub. PyPI download statistics from Snyk and Libraries.io. Framework integrations confirmed by LangChain docs, LlamaIndex docs, Haystack integration page, and Microsoft Semantic Kernel documentation.
confidence.caveats: GitHub star count varies significantly across sources (16K to 42K cited in different places) — the higher figures may include ecosystem repos or be inflated estimates. Chroma Cloud pricing details are not fully public as of February 2026 (serverless model described in general terms only). The Rust rewrite performance claims (4x faster) are from Chroma's own marketing and not independently benchmarked. No Series A funding despite being 3+ years old, which could indicate bootstrapping focus, profitability, or fundraising challenges. Enterprise adoption is not well-documented publicly.
confidence.security_posture: Chroma Cloud offers enterprise security features: end-to-end encryption, role-based access control (RBAC), audit logging, BYOC in customer VPC for data sovereignty. Apache 2.0 open-source license allows full code audit. Self-hosted deployments inherit security of the hosting environment. No specific documentation on vector DB attack surface mitigations (embedding inversion, knowledge base poisoning). SOC 2 or HIPAA certification status not publicly confirmed. GDPR compliance supported via BYOC and EU region deployment options.
